case_info.scenario: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of worsening, painful, right-sided neck swelling with dysphagia, odynophagia, and fever. The neck swelling started with a small lump at the upper neck, which progressively increased in size. There were no symptoms of airway obstruction or aspiration, and the patient denied any constitutional symptoms. She had no history of tuberculous contact, irradiation, preceding trauma, or alleged foreign body impaction in the throat. Examination of the neck showed multiple palpable firm to fluctuant areas of neck swelling over bilateral cervical nodal levels II, III, and V. There was also similar swelling located over the anterior neck, which was fixed and immobile. Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy showed bulging of the right posterior pharyngeal wall at the level of nasopharynx and velopharynx, with pooling of saliva at the pyriform fossae and vallecullae. The vocal folds were normal and mobile. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck showed multiple peripherally enhancing, centrally hypoattenuating lymph nodes; an irregular thyroid mass; and a retropharyngeal fluid collection (Figure 1).
case_info.caption: Axial sections of contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck showing multiple peripherally enhanced cystic lesions involving deep spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space.
case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Axial sections of contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck showing multiple peripherally enhanced cystic lesions involving deep spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space.
case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

1. Mental Demand

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.

She had no history of tuberculous contact, irradiation, preceding trauma, or alleged foreign body impaction in the throat. Examination of the neck showed multiple palpable firm to fluctuant areas of neck swelling over bilateral cervical nodal levels II, III, and V. There was also similar swelling located over the anterior neck, which was fixed and immobile. Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy showed bulging of the right posterior pharyngeal wall at the level of nasopharynx and velopharynx, with pooling of saliva at the pyriform fossae and vallecullae. The vocal folds were normal and mobile. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck showed multiple peripherally enhancing, centrally hypoattenuating lymph nodes; an irregular thyroid mass; and a retropharyngeal fluid collection (Figure 1).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. 2 = Low workload

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

The neck swelling started with a small lump at the upper neck, which progressively increased in size. case_info.caption: Axial sections of contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck showing multiple peripherally enhanced cystic lesions involving deep spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space.
case_info.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is the most aggressive thyroid carcinoma, with an estimated median survival of 5 to 6 months.1It represents 1% to 2% of all thyroid carcinomas, with an annual incidence of 1.2 in 1 000 000.2Due to the rapidity of its progression, up to 63% of patients with ATC present with nodal metastasis in their first presentation, and up to 91% may develop extrathyroidal extension.3Diagnosis of ATC requires tissue-based histopathological assessment either via fine-needle aspiration cytology or tissue biopsy, aided with immunohistochemistry staining.4In the present case, fine-needle aspiration of multiple sites of neck swelling was initially performed because tuberculous infection was originally suspected as a possible cause, as previously reported in Malaysia.5Testing of the aspirated mucoid fluid revealed only atypical cells with microbiological cultures, and mycobacterium tests showed no evidence of infection. Subsequent incisional biopsy of the thyroid gland and level II lymph node showed pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with abnormal mitosis. Immunohistochemistry staining showed strong positivity toward cytokeratin AE1 and AE3, PAX8, p53 with negative thyroid transcription factor-1, and thyroglobulin. Cross-sectional imaging such as a CT scan is invaluable in cases of ATC. Local and regional extent of the tumor with involvement of other critical structures in the neck may be assessed with a high-quality CT scan.3ATC is also commonly associated with extrathyroidal extension, poorly defined margins, and invasion of surrounding cervical structures. Regional lymph node involvement has shown nodal necrosis in most cases of ATC.6This contrasts with lymphadenopathy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which has shown a more homogenous feature of a cystic or solid mass, with the nodes being rarely necrotic.3The CT features of the cystic lesions within the different spaces of the neck, including the retropharyngeal space, are also similar to tuberculous infection and disseminated neck abscess. Our literature review revealed a case previously reported in which CT features of ATC mimicked thyroid abscess.5Thyroid lymphoma may present similarly, including in the present patient who had a rapidly enlarging neck mass and obstructive symptoms. However, the CT features of thyroid lymphoma normally show lesions that are homogenous without calcification or necrosis, in contrast to the case presented herein (Figure 2).7 Management of ATC involves a multidisciplinary approach with the aim of either curative or palliative outcome. Surgical intervention may be considered for several reasons, including relief of aerodigestive obstruction (with or without tracheostomy) or tumor resection. Other options of treatment include radiotherapy with systemic and targeted molecular therapy.4Most patients with ATC, especially those with unresectable tumors, have shown only a 10% survival rate 1 year after diagnosis.8 In the case of this patient, the acute progression of lymphatic involvement, especially of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes, presented a diagnostic conundrum. CT features of hypodense lesions with peripheral enhancement of the lymph nodes and thyroid gland initially pointed toward an infective cause. With a negative microorganism culture and atypical cytology, results from tissue biopsy were invaluable in achieving the diagnosis of ATC. Despite the diagnosis and planning made to manage her condition, the patient died due to complications of hospitalization and tumor progression.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 65-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of worsening, painful, right-sided neck swelling with dysphagia, odynophagia, and fever. The neck swelling started with a small lump at the upper neck, which progressively increased in size. There were no symptoms of airway obstruction or aspiration, and the patient denied any constitutional symptoms. She had no history of tuberculous contact, irradiation, preceding trauma, or alleged foreign body impaction in the throat. Examination of the neck showed multiple palpable firm to fluctuant areas of neck swelling over bilateral cervical nodal levels II, III, and V. There was also similar swelling located over the anterior neck, which was fixed and immobile. Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy showed bulging of the right posterior pharyngeal wall at the level of nasopharynx and velopharynx, with pooling of saliva at the pyriform fossae and vallecullae. The vocal folds were normal and mobile. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the neck showed multiple peripherally enhancing, centrally hypoattenuating lymph nodes; an irregular thyroid mass; and a retropharyngeal fluid collection (Figure 1).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}
